wine.name: Côte-Rôtie La Mouline
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah, the great majority, with about a tenth of Viognier grown among the vines and fermented with it.
wine.sites: La Mouline, a lieu-dit on the Côte Blonde above Ampuis: very old vines on narrow terraces curved round the slope like a Roman amphitheatre, on pale gneiss with silica and a little limestone loess.
wine.making: The Viognier grown among the Syrah goes into the vat with it, and the two ferment together. The wine then spends forty to forty two months in new oak barrels by the house's own sheets, more than three years, before it is bottled at Ampuis.
wine.glass: Violet, raspberry and blackberry over smoked bacon and black pepper, with a lift of apricot skin from the Viognier; silky and perfumed rather than heavy, the new oak folded in as vanilla and toast, on fine, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Open sooner than the house's La Landonne, it wants eight to ten years to absorb its oak, and a strong vintage keeps for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass for the perfume.

label.means: The roasted slope above Ampuis, the northernmost cru of the Rhône: Syrah with up to a fifth Viognier in the vat.
The lieu-dit on the Côte Blonde, first bottled on its own with the 1966 vintage.
The house of Ampuis that grows, makes and bottles the wine.

records.table: From one lieu-dit on the Côte Blonde, La Mouline is E. Guigal's Côte-Rôtie of Syrah fermented with about a tenth of Viognier, then raised more than three years in new oak. Violets and smoked bacon over silk: decant it, and give it a large glass.
records.story: The founder of this house entered the cellars of the Ampuis merchant Vidal-Fleury in 1924, at fourteen, and set up on his own in 1946. In 1961, by the house's account, a sudden blindness, total though it proved temporary, struck him, and his son, then in his teens, took charge. The slope above the village was already told as a story: a lord of Maugiron, it is said, left one hillside to a fair daughter and one to a dark one, and the names Côte Blonde and Côte Brune stuck to rocks that truly differ. With the 1966 vintage the house bottled the old vines of La Mouline, on the Blonde, as a wine of their own. La Landonne followed in 1978 and La Turque in 1985, the trio the trade calls the La La wines, and in 1984 Guigal bought Vidal-Fleury, the house where its founder had begun. In 1995 it bought the Château d'Ampuis by the river, and in 2003 it set up its own cooperage there. The three single vineyards carried the name of Côte-Rôtie far beyond the Rhône. La Mouline remains the lesson in co-fermented Viognier: the white grape lends the perfume, the Syrah gives the frame.

others.name: Côte-Rôtie La Landonne
others.note: From the Côte Brune, Syrah alone, first made in 1978: the firmest and slowest of the three.

others.name: Côte-Rôtie La Turque
others.note: From the Côte Brune with a little Viognier, first made in 1985, the third of the La La wines.

others.name: Côte-Rôtie Château d'Ampuis
others.note: A blend of several lieux-dits, the step below the La La wines, named for the château the house bought in 1995.

traps: La Mouline is on the Côte Blonde; La Landonne and La Turque are on the Côte Brune.
La Landonne is Syrah alone; La Mouline and La Turque are fermented with a little Viognier, which goes into the vat with the Syrah, never into the finished wine.
Vidal-Fleury has been Guigal's since 1984 yet keeps its own label, so a Vidal-Fleury Côte-Rôtie is not a Guigal wine.

wine.name: Hermitage La Chapelle
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, though the appellation would allow a little Marsanne and Roussanne in the vat.
wine.sites: Chiefly Le Méal, on stony terraces in the middle of the south facing hill, and Les Bessards, granite at its western end, with smaller parts from Les Greffieux and Les Rocoules.
wine.making: The grapes are destemmed and each parcel is fermented apart, with three weeks or more on the skins. The blend is then raised for twelve to eighteen months in French oak barrels, a minority of them new, with a share in concrete eggs since the late 2010s.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black olive and smoked bacon over violet, iron and cracked pepper; dense and closed when young, with firm tannin, turning with age to leather, truffle and dried fig.
wine.ageing: Closed for ten to fifteen years after a strong vintage, it then opens slowly; its 1961 and 1978 have lasted for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its heavy sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The single hill above Tain and its appellation: red from Syrah, white from Marsanne and Roussanne.
The house's name for its red, after the chapel of Saint-Christophe at the summit; a name, not a vineyard.
The house name on the label until the 2020 vintage; aîné means the elder, for the founder's son Paul.
The name on the label from the 2021 vintage, when the wine moved to a winery of its own.

records.table: Hermitage La Chapelle, Paul Jaboulet Aîné's red from Le Méal and Les Bessards, takes its name from the chapel of Saint-Christophe on the summit and has been labelled Domaine de La Chapelle since 2021. All Syrah, black olive and smoked meat, it stays closed for ten years or more.
records.story: The hill takes its name from a legend: in the 1220s, the story goes, the knight Gaspard de Stérimberg came home from the crusade against the Albigensians, was granted the slope by Blanche of Castile (1188 to 1252) and lived out his days there as a hermit, at the summit where a chapel now stands. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Bordeaux merchants strengthened their clarets with its wine, for colour and body. The house was founded at Tain in 1834 by Antoine Jaboulet (1807 to 1864) and grew under his sons Paul and Henry; it took its name from Paul, the elder. In 1919 it bought the chapel of Saint-Christophe, and its red Hermitage carries the chapel's name. Through the twentieth century La Chapelle was the Hermitage that drinkers abroad knew by name, and its 1961, with the 1978 beside it, became the measure of what northern Syrah can do with age. After a lean spell in the 1990s the family sold the house in 2006 to the Frey family, and the recovery of La Chapelle dates from that sale. With the 2021 vintage the wine moved to a label and a winery of its own, Domaine de La Chapelle. When a guest names Hermitage, La Chapelle is often the wine they mean.

others.name: Hermitage Le Chevalier de Stérimberg
others.note: The white Hermitage of Marsanne and Roussanne, named for the knight of the legend; from 2021 it too carries the Domaine de La Chapelle label.

others.name: Crozes-Hermitage Domaine de Thalabert
others.note: The house's estate Crozes-Hermitage, Syrah from the larger appellation around the hill.

traps: The chapel names the wine and is a landmark of the hill; La Chapelle is a blend of climats, not a vineyard of that name.
La Chapelle is the red; Le Chevalier de Stérimberg is the white Hermitage.
From the 2021 vintage La Chapelle is labelled Domaine de La Chapelle, not Paul Jaboulet Aîné: the same wine of the hill under a new name.

cards.front: Paul Jaboulet Aîné's La Chapelle: what is the chapel, and is it a vineyard?
cards.back: The chapel of Saint-Christophe at the summit of the hill of Hermitage, which the house bought in 1919; it names the wine and is no vineyard.

wine.name: Hermitage
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah alone; the family keeps its Marsanne and Roussanne for the white Hermitage.
wine.sites: Parcels in several of the hill's climats: Les Bessards on granite at the western end, L'Ermite and Péléat, and Le Méal and Les Rocoules on stonier ground further east.
wine.making: Each parcel is picked, fermented and raised apart, in oak barrels with only a small share of new wood. After some eighteen months the lots are assembled into the one wine, which rests a little longer before it is bottled at Mauves.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black olive and violet over smoked meat, cracked pepper and graphite, with a note of iron and thyme; layered rather than loud, with dense, fine tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved for its first decade, it opens slowly and keeps for thirty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, and pour an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation of the hill above Tain, on the east bank of the Rhône.
The family's merchant label, on wines it buys in; the domaine's own Hermitage does not carry it.

records.table: Rather than bottle each climat, Domaine Jean-Louis Chave blends Les Bessards, L'Ermite, Le Méal and others into a single Hermitage, raising each parcel apart for a year and a half before the blend is made. Black olive, pepper and smoked meat, it is built to last thirty years.
records.story: By the family's own account its growers can be traced to 1481, and the vines have passed from father to son ever since. They worked the granite terraces of the west bank around Mauves, in what became the Saint-Joseph appellation, and in 1865 bought their first parcels across the river on the hill of Hermitage. When the Hermitage appellation was fixed by decree in 1937, the hill was already known by its climats, each with its own ground, from the granite of Les Bessards in the west to the stonier soils further east. Where some houses of the hill came to bottle their climats one by one, the Chaves held to the older idea of Hermitage as a blend of the whole slope, each parcel adding something the others lack. The family also makes a white Hermitage that can outlast the red, a rare vin de paille of grapes dried on straw and, from 1990 and only in chosen years, Cuvée Cathelin, a selection of the red. In the 1990s the son who had taken over the domaine began to reclaim abandoned Saint-Joseph terraces around Mauves. Chave's Hermitage makes the case for blending a hill rather than dividing it.

others.name: Saint-Joseph

wine.name: Cornas
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, as the appellation requires: Cornas admits no white grape at all.
wine.sites: Old vines on steep granite terraces above the village, chiefly Reynard, La Côte, Patou and Sabarotte, blended into this one wine; younger vines go to Renaissance.
wine.making: Whole bunches, stems and all, ferment in concrete vats. The wine is then raised for some twenty months in old oval foudres, with no new oak at all, and bottled unfiltered at the domaine.
wine.glass: Blackberry, tar and black olive over smoked bacon, violet and iron; dark, rugged and tannic in youth, turning with age to smoke, leather and dried thyme.
wine.ageing: Hard and closed for its first eight to ten years, it then softens and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently; a large glass with room for the aromas.

label.means: The appellation facing Valence across the river, red only and Syrah only, on granite.
The legal guarantee that the wine was grown and made under the rules of Cornas.

records.table: Syrah in its old, unpolished form is what Domaine Auguste Clape bottles as Cornas: whole bunches from granite terraces above the village, fermented in concrete and raised in big old foudres without new oak. Black olive, tar and smoke when young, it softens only after eight to ten years.
records.story: Cornas faces Valence across the Rhône, and its name, it is said, comes from a Celtic word for burnt earth, for the sun on its granite terraces. The appellation was drawn in 1938, for red wine alone and Syrah alone. For much of the twentieth century most of the village's harvest was sold in bulk to merchants, and the steep slopes, worked by hand, lost their workers to the factories of the valley. The grower whose name the domaine carries, from a family of Languedoc vignerons, came to Cornas when he married into a family of growers there in 1949. For some years he too sold his wine in bulk; then, in the 1950s, he began to bottle it himself, by most accounts the first grower of the village to do so. He held to the old ways: whole bunches, concrete vats, no new wood and long months in old oval casks. He died in 2018, aged 93, and his son and grandson kept to the same methods. Growers who destem and buy new oak are measured against it, and Clape's Cornas is the wine to taste first to learn the traditional school of northern Syrah.

others.name: Cornas Renaissance
others.note: From the domaine's younger vines: a different bottling, not a selection above the estate Cornas.

others.name: Saint-Péray
others.note: White from Marsanne and Roussanne, from the neighbouring appellation that makes no red.

others.name: Côtes du Rhône
others.note: Syrah from around Cornas sold under the regional name.

traps: Cornas is Syrah only and admits no white grape, unlike Côte-Rôtie, which allows Viognier.
Renaissance is the younger vine Cornas, not a reserve above the estate wine.
Auguste Clape of Cornas has nothing to do with La Clape, the limestone massif of the Languedoc.

cards.front: Domaine Auguste Clape's Cornas: destemmed or whole bunch, and in what wood?
cards.back: Whole bunch, stems and all, raised in large old foudres with no new oak.

cards.front: What may grow beside Syrah in a Cornas, and when was the appellation drawn?

questions.q: A guest compares a young Clape Cornas with a polished, new oak Cornas from another grower. What sets the Clape apart in the cellar?

questions.exp: Clape ferments whole bunches and raises the wine in big old foudres with no new oak; Cornas allows no Viognier, and carbonic maceration is the method of Beaujolais.

wine.name: Condrieu Coteau de Vernon
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Viognier alone, as the appellation requires.
wine.sites: Coteau de Vernon, the hillside above the town of Condrieu: old vines on terraces of biotite granite facing south and south east.
wine.making: The grapes are pressed whole and the juice is settled cold, then fermented in oak, a minority of it new. The wine is raised on its fine lees for twelve to eighteen months before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Apricot skin, white peach and honeysuckle over violet, white pepper and wet granite; full and silky, yet held in line by a stony, faintly bitter finish rather than any sweetness.
wine.ageing: Pleasing young, it gains honey, dried apricot and a waxy depth over eight to ten years, where most Condrieu is drunk young.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The appellation of Viognier alone on the granite of the northern Rhône; most is dry, though the rules allow a sweet style.
A lieu-dit, the hillside above the town, not an appellation of its own.

records.table: Coteau de Vernon is Domaine Georges Vernay's Condrieu from old Viognier on granite terraces above the town, fermented in oak and raised on its lees for a year and more. Dry, with apricot, violet and a stony, slightly bitter finish, it is a Condrieu for the cellar.
records.story: Sweet Condrieu was long the custom of the hill, and its steep granite terraces were hard to work. The appellation was drawn in 1940, beside the single estate of Château-Grillet, which had been given an appellation of its own in 1936. After the war the terraces emptied, and by the 1950s, as Inter Rhône tells it, the vineyard had all but vanished. The grower whose name the domaine carries held on to his vines through those lean years, and when he died in 2017 the obituaries credited him with saving Viognier from extinction. Inter Rhône dates the revival of the appellation to the 1980s and to the work of a handful of growers, and Viognier was later planted from California to the Languedoc. Coteau de Vernon, the old vines on the hill above the town, became the domaine's flagship, made to age rather than to drink at once. His daughter took charge in 1996. Most Condrieu is drunk within a few years; Coteau de Vernon was made to be kept, and it shows what the grape his family kept alive can become.
